```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE)
```

A smooth fitted with an increasing or convex shape constraint can still have
interval endpoints that lack that shape. `shape_intervals()` adjusts the
endpoints to satisfy the chosen restrictions at the evaluation points.
For restrictions that apply to a whole function, such as requiring its
integral to equal one, `shape_confidence_set()` instead records the coefficient
vectors satisfying those restrictions and the supplied uncertainty bounds.

We first apply these functions to supplied intervals and fitted smooths, then
explain what the transformations imply for coverage. The examples use {gratia},
{mgcv} and {ggplot2}, which we load below.

```{r packages}
library("gratia")
load_mgcv()
library("ggplot2")
```

## Apply shape restrictions to existing intervals

`shape_intervals()` works directly on estimates and interval limits that you
supply. It can impose non-negative values, increasing
or decreasing values, and convex or concave curvature. To impose increasing
values it sorts the supplied values along the relevant coordinate. To impose
convexity it finds the largest convex curve lying below those values; this is
called the *greatest convex minorant*. Concavity uses the corresponding
operation with signs reversed. These operations follow
[Chen and colleagues (2021)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v22/20-513.html),
building on [monotone rearrangement](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/asp030).
The following small example requests endpoints that are both increasing and
convex over `x`. The deliberately uneven initial estimates make the adjustment
visible in the returned values.

```{r supplied-band}
x <- c(0, 0.1, 0.35, 0.7, 1)
estimate <- c(0.1, 0.3, 0.2, 0.8, 1.1)
shaped <- shape_intervals(
  estimate, estimate - 0.3, estimate + 0.3,
  data = data.frame(x = x), constraints = list(x = c("m+", "c+")),
  interval = "simultaneous", level = 0.95
)
shaped
attr(shaped, "interval_info")
```

The returned table contains `.estimate`, `.lower_ci` and `.upper_ci`, with
method information in `interval_info`. Here `level = 0.95` labels the starting
limits. For an analysis, supply limits from an uncertainty calculation that
supports the stated coverage. The final section shows how the adjustment can
change that coverage.

The supported codes are `"+"` for non-negative values, `"m+"` and `"m-"` for
increasing and decreasing values, and `"c+"` and `"c-"` for convexity and
concavity. Increasing and decreasing include flat sections. A complete
Cartesian grid can have monotonicity in several directions and curvature in
at most one direction. These are directional restrictions: convexity along
one coordinate does not establish joint convexity of a surface.

Rows may be unordered and coordinates may be irregularly spaced. Convexity
uses slopes computed from the actual coordinate differences. The sorting step
gives each distinct coordinate equal weight, even when distances between
coordinates differ. Duplicate grid rows and incomplete combinations of
coordinates are rejected.

## Add shape-constrained intervals to a fitted smooth

For supported `mgcv::scasm()` smooths, request the adjustment with
`interval_method = "shape"`. Here `x` ranges over the unit interval and the
mean response is an increasing, convex quadratic function of `x`. Independent
Gaussian noise has standard deviation 0.2. We fit those two shape restrictions
and construct a simultaneous band using a Gaussian approximation to coefficient
uncertainty, selected by `shape_source = "gaussian"`.

```{r fit-curve}
set.seed(1701)
d <- data.frame(x = runif(200))
d$y <- 2 * d$x + 4 * d$x^2 + rnorm(nrow(d), sd = 0.2)
m <- scasm(
  y ~ s(x, bs = "sc", xt = c("m+", "c+"), k = 6),
  data = d, bs = 0
)
curve <- smooth_estimates(
  m, select = "s(x)", interval = "simultaneous",
  interval_method = "shape", shape_source = "gaussian",
  n = 100, n_sim = 2000, seed = 1702
)
draw(curve)
```

This displays the smooth on the model scale, with the centring used in the fit.
Its band describes uncertainty in the smooth itself. Use
`overall_uncertainty = FALSE` if you set that argument explicitly. Shape
intervals apply to the fitted smooth in its original units and require any
effect shifts and transformations to be omitted. The standard errors in `curve`
describe the calculation before the shape adjustment. Read the adjusted limits
directly from `.lower_ci` and `.upper_ci`.

Default plot captions show the basis and named shapes. The interval source,
level and coverage information remain in the result's `interval_info`
attribute and in this documentation.

The Gaussian source uses the model's approximate Bayesian covariance by
default. Set `frequentist = TRUE` to use the covariance of the coefficient
estimators. `unconditional = TRUE` requests the correction for smoothing
parameter uncertainty when available. The chosen covariance determines the
starting band. The shape adjustment changes its limits and leaves the
underlying coefficient distribution as it was.

The same method selection is available through `draw()`, `assemble()` and
`confint()` for supported smooth components. For example, `draw(m,
interval = "simultaneous", interval_method = "shape", n_sim = 2000,
seed = 1702)` computes and displays the intervals in one call. Select smooths
whose named restrictions are still in force after fitting. Use an explicit
confidence set for more general coefficient constraints, as described below.
Numeric `by` variables are unsupported because multiplying the smooth by a
varying value can change its shape.

If you supply general coefficient inequalities in `pc`, mgcv can use those
in place of the named restrictions in `xt`. In that case, the plot caption
identifies the requested restrictions as dropped and shape intervals are
unavailable. Point equality constraints are supported when the named
restrictions still apply. A constraint on the smooth itself need not imply
the same constraint on its derivative, so bases that evaluate derivatives
are unsupported.

For transformed covariates, shape is asserted in the coordinates used by the
model. For example, a restriction on `s(log(x), ...)` concerns `log(x)`;
curvature in that coordinate need not be curvature in `x`.

## Constrain one direction of a smooth surface

For a surface, shape restrictions can apply along one covariate while the
other remains unrestricted. The example below has an increasing exponential
effect of `x`, a quadratic effect of `z`, and independent Gaussian noise with
standard deviation 0.15. We constrain the fitted surface to increase with `x`
at each fixed `z`.

This construction requires B-spline margins fitted with `np = FALSE`, which
keeps their original parameterisation, and evaluation within their fitted
domains. Both `"sc"` and ordinary `"bs"` margins are supported. These
requirements ensure that the coefficient restrictions imply the stated shape
of the surface.

```{r fit-tensor}
set.seed(1703)
surface_data <- data.frame(x = runif(300), z = runif(300))
surface_data$y <- exp(1.5 * surface_data$x) + surface_data$z^2 +
  rnorm(nrow(surface_data), sd = 0.15)
surface_model <- scasm(
  y ~ te(x, z, bs = c("sc", "bs"), k = c(5, 5),
    xt = list("m+", NULL), np = FALSE),
  data = surface_data, bs = 0
)
surface <- smooth_estimates(
  surface_model, select = "te(x,z)", interval = "simultaneous",
  interval_method = "shape", n_2d = 30, dist = 0,
  n_sim = 2000, seed = 1704
)
draw(surface)
```

The surface and its interval limits increase with `x` at each fixed `z`.
`dist = 0` keeps every combination of the two grid coordinates, as required
for the adjustment. Keep the evaluation grid within the fitted B-spline domains.

Automatic curvature inference additionally requires regular knots and a
sufficient spline degree. In mgcv 1.9-4, the raw second coefficient differences
used by `"c+"` and `"c-"` do not ensure spline curvature with arbitrary irregular
knots. Equal spacing is checked to rounding precision, because even small
departures can reverse curvature when a coefficient restriction binds.
Requests with those knots are rejected. The low-level operator can
still enforce a justified shape directly on an irregular evaluation grid;
that is a separate statement from the shape implied by fitted inequalities.
Requests for multiple curvature directions are also rejected because a later
convexification can destroy curvature enforced in an earlier direction.

## Use bootstrap limits as the starting intervals

With `bs > 0`, a `scasm()` fit stores bootstrap coefficient vectors that satisfy
the fitted constraints in `model$bs`. The bootstrap holds smoothing parameters
fixed and perturbs the working likelihood from the final fit. The intervals
from mgcv use percentiles of curves evaluated at each grid point. When
`svar.only` is present, mgcv also adjusts the limits using the mean difference
between Bayesian and frequentist standard errors.
Percentiles of convex functions need not be convex, and the endpoint adjustment
can alter restrictions further.

`interval_method = "shape", shape_source = "bootstrap"` adjusts these pointwise
limits using the same shape rules. Supply a model with stored bootstrap draws
and keep `frequentist = FALSE` and `unconditional = FALSE` to match the mgcv
calculation. This option supports pointwise starting limits only. Bootstrap
coverage can be poor at the boundary of the allowed shapes, for instance when
a curve constrained to be increasing is actually flat.
[Andrews (2000)](https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-0262.00114).

## Keep an integral or other coefficient restriction fixed

An integral equality cannot generally be assigned to two different ordered
endpoint curves. If both have integral one and their difference is
nonnegative, that difference must have integral zero. A useful uncertainty
description instead retains a set of whole functions.

`shape_confidence_set()` stores the intersection

\[
\{b: L\leq Xb\leq U,\quad A_{\mathrm{in}}b\geq b_{\mathrm{in}},
\quad Cb=d\}.
\]

Here $b$ is a candidate coefficient vector. The prediction matrix $X$ maps it
to curve values, which must lie between the supplied limits $L$ and $U$.
The other two conditions specify inequalities and equalities on $b$.

In the following example, the three coefficients give the values of a piecewise
linear curve at `x = c(0, 0.5, 1)`. The positive weights below give its exact
integral over `[0, 1]`, which is required to equal one. We combine that equality
with non-negative coefficients and bounds from zero to two, then test two
candidate curves for membership of the resulting set. A spline analysis
would supply its own prediction matrix and integrals of basis functions.

```{r equality-set}
weights <- c(0.25, 0.5, 0.25)
region <- shape_confidence_set(
  X = diag(3), lower = c(0, 0, 0), upper = c(2, 2, 2),
  Ain = diag(3),
  C = matrix(weights, nrow = 1), d = 1,
  level = 0.95, interpretation = "confidence", band_type = "simultaneous"
)
in_shape_set(region, c(0.5, 1, 1.5))
in_shape_set(region, c(0.5, 1, 1))
```

The first candidate satisfies the integral equality; the second does not.
`in_shape_set()` checks membership with a documented absolute tolerance. It
does not generate draws or find the largest and smallest possible values.
The restrictions can also be inconsistent, leaving an empty set, so check
that they express the intended scientific constraints.

As in the earlier interval example, `level` and `band_type` describe the bounds
you supply. If the true coefficients satisfy the restrictions, intersecting
their allowed values with a simultaneous band preserves that band's coverage
event. Pointwise limits alone do not provide a simultaneous confidence region.

The set retains linear equalities and inequalities involving several
coefficients together. It describes which functions are allowed by the
restrictions and supplied bounds. To draw functions from a Bayesian posterior,
one would also need to specify that posterior on the allowed coefficients; see
[Hazelton and Turlach (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.csda.2011.04.018)
for shape-constrained penalised splines. Likewise,
[Dümbgen (2003)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6466) constructs calibrated bands
using multiscale tests in a Gaussian white-noise model. Those calibration
results are distinct from the finite-grid endpoint transformation implemented
here.

## How shape restrictions affect coverage

Write $T$ for the complete shape operator and $f$ for target values satisfying
the requested shape on the grid. The operator preserves order and fixes $f$.
Consequently,

\[
L \leq f \leq U \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
T(L) \leq T(f)=f \leq T(U),
\]

where each inequality holds at every grid point together. Thus if the original
band contains the target at every grid point, the adjusted band also contains
it at every point. The same preservation of coverage applies to a credible
band if the posterior is defined on curves that satisfy the constraints.
The band's greatest width over the grid cannot increase, although it can
become wider at individual points.

This implication does not establish nominal coverage for the initial band.
In particular, transforming separately calibrated pointwise limits does not
preserve their marginal coverage at each point: sorting moves information
between coordinates. `interval = "pointwise"` records this source calibration
without assigning new pointwise coverage to the result. Penalisation bias or
an inadequate covariance approximation can also affect initial coverage; the
shape operation does not correct either problem.

Connecting the returned points by straight lines preserves the curve shape,
but the coverage statement concerns the grid points only. An adjusted limit
curve can also differ from any spline in the original basis, so the limits
need not satisfy the centring conditions imposed on the fitted spline.

### Coverage in simulation studies

The experiment in `notes/scasm/shape-coverage.R` examines two settings:
Gaussian intervals with known variance, and intervals estimated from fitted
`scasm()` models. It uses 2,000 repetitions per known-variance scenario and
400 attempted fits per `scasm()` scenario, including exactly flat and exactly
linear true functions. At 95% coverage,
the binomial Monte Carlo standard error is about 0.5 percentage points for
2,000 repetitions and 1.1 percentage points for 400 successful fits.
The `scasm()` experiment applies `shape_intervals()` to fitted response curves
including their intercepts, so the true and fitted curves use the same
reference level.

For a nearly flat increasing truth, the smallest marginal coverage over grid
points fell from 93.65% to 38.00% after transforming Gaussian pointwise limits.
Using an initially calibrated simultaneous band, whole-grid coverage instead
changed from 94.85% to 95.75%. No originally covering whole-grid band lost
coverage in any of the 49,182 paired transformations across the experiment.
These results illustrate why the distinction between pointwise intervals and
simultaneous bands matters: preserving an already covering whole band does
not preserve coverage at each individual point after sorting.

The `scasm()` examples also show that the initial uncertainty calculation still
matters after imposing shape restrictions. For a true curve close to the
boundary of the increasing, convex restrictions, the
transformed Gaussian simultaneous band covered the whole grid in 313 of 342
returned fits: 91.52%, with Monte Carlo standard error 1.51 percentage points.
The other 58 attempts raised upstream fitting errors, so this estimate is
conditional on a model being returned. The saved reports record the fitting
errors and warnings separately. Changing the smoothing penalty also changed
local bias, but that comparison did not assess interval coverage or width.
The shape adjustment itself does not correct smoothing bias.
